response_text: When the user invokes the OS function osCreateThread(thread_function, argument) or osCreateThreadWithDeadline(thread_function, argument, deadline), the process of passing arguments into threads starts. Usually, the argument is a pointer to data that the thread will require while it is running. Since the thread will access this data asynchronously after creation, the user must make sure this argument points to valid memory that will be accessible for the duration of the thread, such as a global variable, static variable, or dynamically allocated memory. When the OS receives this thread creation request, it performs several critical steps to ensure the argument reaches the thread correctly. First, the OS allocates a stack for the new thread using alloc_stack(), then constructs an initial stack frame that mimics what the ARM Cortex-M processor expects when entering a function. This stack frame contains 16 registers worth of data, with the most crucial being the Program Counter (PC) set to the thread function's address, and importantly, register R0 set to the argument value using *(--sp) = (uint32_t)arg. The OS then stores this prepared stack pointer in the thread's control block along with the timeslice and other metadata, making the thread ready for execution. The ARM Architecture Procedure Call Standard (AAPCS), which stipulates that the first function argument is always passed in register R0, is what makes the mechanism function. The hardware automatically loads all of the saved registers from the thread's stack, including R0, which contains the argument value, when the thread is finally scheduled and the processor executes a context switch. The function receives this R0 value as its first parameter as the processor branches to the thread function's entry point, just like if it had been called normally by another function. Through the standard void* arg parameter, the thread function can instantly access its argument thanks to the OS's stack frame construction and the processor's calling convention, allowing threads to receive initialization data, configuration structures.\n
